faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and an award rate?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage is the base rate for employees not covered by an award or agreement. From 1 July 2026 it is $26.44 per hour for a 38-hour week. Award rates are set by the Fair Work Commission for specific industries and occupations, and are often higher than the minimum wage. You can find the correct award rate using the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay guides.

faqs.q: How is casual loading applied to the hourly rate?
faqs.a: Casual employees are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the minimum hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. For example, the National Minimum Wage casual rate is $33.05 per hour ($26.44 × 1.25). When using a calculator, you should enter the base hourly rate and select the casual loading option, not a rate that already includes loading.

faqs.q: Does the annual pay estimate include superannuation?
faqs.a: No, superannuation is paid on top of your gross pay. The super guarantee rate is 12% of ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. The annual estimate shows your gross salary before super; your employer pays super separately.

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Hourly Pay to Annual Salary and Wages

When you're comparing job offers or planning your budget, understanding how your hourly rate translates into annual **salary and wages** is essential. In Australia, the standard full-time week is 38 hours, and most annual calculations use 52 weeks per year. The formula is straightforward:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For example, if you earn $30 per hour and work 38 hours each week, your annual gross pay would be $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This figure is before tax, Medicare levy, and superannuation.

### Why 38 Hours?

The Fair Work Commission defines the ordinary hours of work for a full-time employee as 38 per week under the National Employment Standards. Many awards and agreements also use this standard. If your hours differ, adjust the formula accordingly. For part-time or casual work, use your typical weekly hours.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

The **National Minimum Wage** from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. This applies to employees not covered by an award or registered agreement. However, most workers are covered by an industry or occupation award, which sets higher minimum pay rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides [pay guides](/blog) that list the correct rates for each award classification.

Award rates often include penalty rates for weekends, evenings, or overtime. The annual conversion here assumes the same rate every week, so it does not account for penalty rates or allowances. For a more precise estimate, use the [timesheet](/) on this site, which lets you enter your base hourly rate and add casual loading if applicable.

### Casual Loading

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid sick leave or annual leave. For the National Minimum Wage, the casual rate is $33.05 per hour ($26.44 × 1.25). When using our calculator, enter the base rate (e.g., $26.44) and check the casual loading box – do not enter $33.05 directly.

### Fortnightly Pay

Many employers pay fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross pay, multiply your weekly pay by 2. For a $30/hour employee working 38 hours per week, weekly pay is $1,140, so fortnightly pay is $2,280. This can help you match your budget cycle.

### Tax and Medicare

Your annual gross pay is subject to income tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:

- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus a Medicare levy of 2% (based on 2025–26 single reduction thresholds, as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed at the time of this reference). The [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page can help you estimate your net income.

### Superannuation

Super guarantee contributions are paid by your employer on top of your salary and wages. From 1 July 2026, the rate is 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For example, if your annual gross is $80,000, your employer must contribute an extra $9,600 to your super fund. This is not deducted from your pay – it is an additional benefit.

### Example: National Minimum Wage vs Award

Consider a retail employee covered by the General Retail Industry Award. The minimum hourly rate for a Level 1 adult employee is higher than the National Minimum Wage. Using the award rate (say $28.50 per hour) in the formula gives annual gross of $28.50 × 38 × 52 = $56,316. The National Minimum Wage would give $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,245. Always check the correct award rate via the Fair Work Ombudsman's [reference tables](/data).

### Important Notes

This annual estimate assumes:
- The same hourly rate every week (no penalty rates, overtime, or allowances)
- No unpaid overtime
- No salary sacrifice arrangements
- Super is paid on top, not included in the gross figure

For a personalised calculation that accounts for casual loading, use the [timesheet](/) on this site. You can also explore [average pay](/topics/average-pay) data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics to see how your rate compares nationally.

Understanding your **salary and wages** in annual terms helps you negotiate offers, plan tax, and set financial goals. Whether you're on the National Minimum Wage or an award, the conversion is a simple but powerful tool.
